title: Workers paid more contributions three months on from Payday Super
full_text:
Monthly payments into Australian workers’ superannuation accounts have more than doubled since Payday Super began on 1 July, with preliminary ASFA research estimating around 7 million workers have moved away from quarterly contributions.
Around 54 million super payments were processed in August, compared with a monthly average of around 25 million in 2025–26. ASFA expects transaction numbers to remain around the August level as contributions become more evenly distributed throughout the year.
The association estimates workers previously receiving quarterly super payments are now predominantly receiving contributions weekly or fortnightly, although some have moved to monthly payments. A further 2-3 million workers are likely to have shifted from monthly contributions to weekly or fortnightly payments.
ASFA chief executive Mary Delahunty said the early figures showed the reform was working as intended.
“Payday Super was designed to make sure super is paid at the same time as wages. Two months in, the data shows that is happening for millions of workers.
“When super is paid sooner, it is invested sooner and earns returns for longer. A 25-year-old on average wages will have around $5,000 more in retirement just from more frequent payments. It has also made it less likely that workers will miss out on being paid the super they are entitled to,” Delahunty said.
ASFA’s paper drew on contribution message data collected by the Gateway Network Governance Body, which monitors contributions made through SuperStream, alongside the experience of member funds.
The data showed contribution messages increased from 27 million in May to 34 million in June, before reaching 64 million in July as employers made their final quarterly payments alongside their first payday contributions.
Employees of small businesses are seeing the largest change because their employers were more likely to pay super quarterly before the reform.
A 2022 employer survey cited in the paper found 49 per cent of businesses with one to four employees paid super quarterly, compared with 13 per cent of employers with at least 200 employees. ASFA noted payment frequency may have increased since that survey.
One super fund with many small business employers recorded 3.5 times as many employer contribution transactions after Payday Super began. A fund with a more diverse employer base received around twice as many, while a fund with more members working for large employers recorded around 1.35 times as many.
The latter two funds also reported contribution values around 1.4 times their previous levels, reflecting the transitional increase in payments.
Industries dominated by small businesses, including building and construction, road transport, cafes and restaurants, hairdressing and beauty, and cleaning, are also among those with the highest levels of unpaid super.
The Australian Taxation Office estimates $6.2 billion in super guarantee contributions went unpaid in 2022–23.
“Younger Aussies, tradies, and hospo staff are among the workers most likely to miss out on super because of unpaid contributions. They are the people Payday Super was designed to protect.
“Under the quarterly system, workers often noticed missing super four to six months after they earned it. By then the business may have gone into liquidation, and the super may never be recovered. Employers now have seven business days after payday to get super into a worker’s fund, so a missed payment can be identified within weeks, not months,” Delahunty said.
ASFA’s paper estimated that recovering unpaid super in a typical case involving a 35-year-old could leave their retirement balance more than $30,000 better off in today’s dollars.
While the research anticipates earlier identification of unpaid contributions, it cautions that unpaid super will continue because of factors including sham contracting, the cash economy and employer insolvencies.
The association also expects smaller, more frequent contributions and earlier intervention to help employers avoid accumulating large super guarantee liabilities, while integrating contributions more closely with payroll.
Delahunty encouraged workers to compare their super account records with their payslips.
“Payday Super works in part because it lets you check your super statements against your payslip each pay cycle. It’s important to log into your super account and check that your super is actually being paid into your account, and not just being listed on your payslip. If something looks wrong, talk to your employer first, and then the ATO if you need to,” Delahunty said.
Despite the increase in payment frequency, Payday Super has not changed the super guarantee contribution rate of 12 per cent or who employers are required to pay super for.
ASFA expects APRA’s September 2026 quarter statistics to show a substantial one-off increase in the value of employer contributions because of the overlapping payments in July, before returning to customary levels from the December quarter.
Employer super guarantee contributions averaged around $34 billion a quarter in 2025–26, with the reform expected to distribute payments more evenly across the year.
